citation: Bert Daelemans, “Le Caché nous relève en se révélant. La révélation rédemptrice dans les Hymnes sur la Nativité de St. Éphrem,” Orientalia Christiana Periodica 78:1 (2012): 29–80.

data.title: Le Caché nous relève en se révélant. La révélation rédemptrice dans les Hymnes sur la Nativité de St. Éphrem
data.abstractNote: This is the second of two articles discussing the revelatory aspect of divine redemption in Ephrem’s Hymns on the Nativity. Complementary to the detailed study of the third hymn of this collection (OCP 77 [2011] 351-398), this article presents the results of a comparative study of recurrent terms in the whole collection on the Nativity, making references to Ephrem’s entire oeuvre. The first part examines three terminological groups concerning the revelatory aspect of redemption, namely ksy’/gly’; dnš’; and lbwš’/’sṭl šwbḥ’. The second part focuses on three terminological groups emphasizing the redemptive aspect of revelation, namely ’rkn/nḥt/z‘r; ḥyl’; phgr’. Finally, a synthesis of both articles collects their results, as the importance of verbs in Ephrem’s poetical theology, the centrality of ḥyl’, and the omnipresence of revelation in the Hymns of the Nativity. For Ephrem, God remains the absolute hidden Mystery, who noetically reveals Godself through a Christological aesthetics, pedagogically adapted to our senses, and soteriologically uplifting, giving us life.

data.abstractNote: Two Arabic accounts are edited, translated and analysed for the first time in this paper. In the first, the Chaldean priest ʿAbd al‑Aḥad describes the stages of his almost year‑long round trip (October 1707-June 1708) between his native Amid/Diyarbakır and the Holy Land. The second, shorter and more factual, gives the death toll from a plague in the Diyarbakır region in 1712. These accounts provide a wealth of demographic, historical, linguistic and toponymic information. But they are also of interest beyond their content, in that they have no equivalent in the pre-modern literary tradition of the Christians of Syria-Mesopotamia. This article aims to show that the two texts composed by ʿAbd al‑Aḥad are eloquent witnesses to developments taking place on both a literary and a codicological level. These developments occurred in the particular context of the 17th and 18th centuries, which saw the affirmation of Eastern Churches in communion with Rome. These two ‘personal’ narratives thus raise new questions about the role played respectively by confession and cultural practices in the way that history is recorded.

data.title: Towards a New Edition of Julian’s Contra Galilaeos: Assessing the Material from the Syriac Transmission of Cyril’s Contra Ivlianvm
data.abstractNote: Emperor Julian's three-book treatise Contra Galilaeos survives solely in those Christian sources that quoted it in order to respond to its forceful attack on Christianity. The bulk of these survivals comes from Cyril of Alexandria's twenty-book Contra Iulianum. The recent publication of the first modern critical edition of Cyril's work creates the occasion for a fresh study of the remnants of Julian's text that can be recovered from it. This is especially true for Books 11–20 of Cyril's treatise that are themselves lost and survive only in quotations in later Greek and Syriac sources. The present article undertakes a reassessment of the Julianic material preserved via the Syriac transmission of Contra Iulianum, including several passages hitherto unknown or ignored in earlier studies of Julian's treatise. It provides the Syriac text and English translation of eight passages and contextualizes them in the wider argumentative aim of Contra Galilaeos.

data.abstractNote: Approximately one-third of the Oration to the Greeks composed by Tatian the Assyrian is devoted to exposing the origin and current activity of demons in human affairs. The primary goal of the present article is to elucidate the source and logic of Tatian's demonology, specifically as it relates to astrological fate and pharmacology, the two "hostile devices of the demented demons" that he denounces. I argue, first, that his focus upon these two areas is not by chance, but is due to the influence of 1 Enoch, since, like 1 Enoch, he holds that these domains of human expertise derive from malevolent heavenly beings. I argue, second, that Tatian's criticisms of both astrology and pharmacology are structurally analogous insofar as he claims both are purely the product of demonic contrivance. As a result, these seeming areas of knowledge are in fact based upon nothing real or natural about the world but are instead arbitrary and nonsensical. Moreover, Tatian's emphasis upon demonic delusion serves the polemical goal of his Oration in an additional way, since it casts the demons as a foil for Tatian himself. Unlike the demons, whom he compares to bandits, Tatian speaks as a representative of the true world order and its one legitimate ruler, and he offers his own Oration as a kind of harsh logotherapy that can accomplish the very thing the demons mendaciously claim to be able to effect through astrology and pharmacology.

data.abstractNote: "Das allein im Matthäusevangelium überlieferte Jesuswort: "Sehet zu, dassihr keinen dieser Geringen verachtet; denn ich sage euch: Ihre Engel im Himmel sehen immerfort das Antlitz meines Vaters, der im Himmel ist!" data.abstractNote: For the "determination" of the dominical logoi as cited in the original text of the Greek Didascalia, these "studies" propose and apply new and more adequate methodologies than have been employed heretofore; and for the "evaluation" of said logoi they apply the formgeschichtlich and redaktionsgeschichtlich methodologies -methodologies that have not been employed (in the study of the Didascalist's citations) heretofore. As a result of the application of these methodologies, it has been demonstrated that the Didascalist's immediate source - the "Gospel," as the Didascalist himself refers to it again and again - is not to be defined as any individual Gospel (e g. the Gospel of Matthew), or any collection of Gospels (e g. the Synoptics), nor is it to be defined as a "harmony" of the Gospels. Kather it is to be defined as the entire body of "Gospel" traditions available to the Didascalist - a body of traditions that consisted, as far as the evidence in the Didascalia itself will allow definition, in the main, of a collection or, more probably, collections of logoi Jesu - collections which, like the collections of logoi Jesu, Q, and the Gospel of Thomas, contained comparatively little, if any gospel narrative material. All of the dominical logoi analyzed in these "studies" probably derive inmmediately from such collections of logoi Jesu, e.g., the logoi cited at Didasc. I.1.7 and III.11.3 (Study, II), Didasc. II.16.1 and VI.14.4 (Study, IV), Didasc. II.36.9 (Study, VI), and Didasc. VI.13.3 and VI.14.8 (Study, VII) undoubtedly derive immediately from such collections; the logos cited at Didasc. I.1.4 (Stzldy, I ) probably derives immediately from such collections; and the logoi cited at Didasc. I.6.10, II.34.7, VI.12.11, and VI.17.6 (Study, III), and Didasc. II.20.1 and II.32.2 (Study, V) likely derive irrznzediately from such collections. Those collections consisted of logoi Jesu that were derived ultimately from a variety of sources: (i) the canonical Gospels, e.g.. the logoi cited at Didasc. I.6.10, II.34.7, VI.12.11, and VI.17.6 (Study, III) and Didasc. VI.13.3 and VI.14.8 (Study, VII) clearly derive ultimately from the Gospel of Matthew, and the logoi cited at Didasc. II.20.1 and II.32.2 (Study, V) clearly derives ultimately from the Gospel of Luke: and (ii) non-canonical sources, e.g., the logoi cited at Didasc. I.1.7 and III.11.3 (Study, II), Didasc. II.16.1 and VI.14.4 (Study, IV), and Didasc. II.36.9 (Study, VI) clearly derive ultirrzately from a source, or sources, quite independent of the Synoptic Gospels, though, in the case of the logoi cited at Didasc. I.1.7 and III.11.3 (Study, II) and Didasc. II.16.1 and VI.14.4 (Study, IV), parallel to them.
